South-east London · Walking route

Blackheath to Greenwich: the slow way down the hill

Start with village shops, cross the open heath and enter Greenwich Park from above. The famous view comes later; the quieter route towards it is the real pleasure.

By Paolo Pastorino27 September 20266 min read
At a glance
Start
Blackheath station
Finish
Greenwich station, DLR or pier
Distance
About 5–7 km depending on detours
Allow
2 hours direct; 3–5 hours with stops ↗

Most Greenwich visits begin at the river and climb towards the Observatory. Starting in Blackheath reverses the effort and improves the story. You arrive quickly from central London, spend time in a neighbourhood with its own rhythm, cross a wide patch of sky and then descend through Greenwich Park as the city gradually appears.

The route is simple enough to improvise. Its strength lies in the optional turns: a second-hand bookshop, a flower garden, an old oak, a less crowded viewpoint and one or two exceptional interiors at the end.

Begin in Blackheath, not at the station exit

Blackheath is around fifteen minutes by train from London Bridge, but do not hurry straight towards the park. The streets near the station reward a short circuit: independent shops, cafés and the kind of local bookshop where browsing can easily become the first delay of the day.

Then cross the heath. The openness is the point. Canary Wharf and the City appear on the horizon, but the immediate landscape refuses the density usually associated with London. On windy days the exposure is real; bring an extra layer even when the centre feels mild.

Ranger’s House stands near the edge of Greenwich Park and can become a separate visit when open. If not, use it as a landmark and enter the park nearby.

Take the quieter side of Greenwich Park

The direct route to the Observatory is obvious and often busy. A better first move is through the Flower Garden, where the paths feel more enclosed and the park reveals itself gradually. From there, look for Queen Elizabeth’s Oak. The ancient tree has long since fallen, but its remains and the stories attached to it make a surprisingly effective pause.

One Tree Hill is the essential detour. Its viewpoint sits east of Observatory Hill and looks across the Thames from a quieter angle. The path is steep, but the view preserves more foreground and feels less like a queue for the same photograph. New seating makes it a good place to stop.

If mobility or time is limited, remain on the main paths and head towards the familiar General Wolfe viewpoint instead. The route still works; it simply becomes more direct.

Descend through layers of Greenwich

From the hill, the geometry of the Queen’s House and Old Royal Naval College lines up towards the river. Walking down converts a famous panorama into a sequence of real spaces. The Queen’s House is worth entering when open, particularly for the Tulip Stairs, whose blue spiral is far more delicate than the building’s formal exterior suggests.

Continue to the Old Royal Naval College. The grounds are free to cross and remain impressive even without a ticket. The Chapel of St Peter and St Paul is open daily during normal visitor hours; the Painted Hall requires paid admission, currently sold with year-round return access. Its scale makes it a strong finale if you still have energy.

Greenwich Market is nearby, but it is better treated as an optional reward than an obligatory ending. On crowded weekends, a riverside walk or a quieter café may be more pleasant.

Distance and timing

The basic walk is roughly 5 kilometres, depending on your route through the park. With the Flower Garden, One Tree Hill, interiors and Blackheath browsing, it can easily become 7 kilometres and occupy most of a day. Allow at least two hours without stops and three to five for the version that makes the journey worthwhile.

The overall direction is downhill, but there are short climbs and some steep paths. After heavy rain, softer routes in the park may be muddy. Pedestrian gate times change seasonally, so check the Royal Parks page if you plan a very early or late walk.

Why this direction is better

Ending at Greenwich gives you more options: trains, DLR, buses or a boat back towards central London. More importantly, the route builds naturally. It begins with ordinary local life, opens onto landscape and finishes among some of London’s grandest architecture.

Greenwich’s famous view is not the destination. It is the moment when the whole walk finally explains where you have been going.

Take the slow way down. The landmarks will still be there, but they will arrive with context rather than all at once.

Practical information was checked against the sources below. Always confirm with the venue before a time- or access-sensitive visit.
